items.title: Man Who Orchestrated Tupac Shakur Murder Sentenced to 40 Years to Life in Prison
items.summary:
A Nevada court has sentenced Duane "Keffe D" Davis to 40 years to life in prison for his role in orchestrating the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur, closing out a case that sat unresolved for nearly three decades.

Shakur's family addressed the court before the sentence came down. His sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, told the court that "the loss of Tupac crippled my family emotionally," describing a brother who "dedicated his career to the advancement of his people" and "was truly my shining star." His brother Mopreme Shakur spoke separately about everything the rapper never got to do. "Pac didn't have a chance to have kids," he said. "He didn't have a chance to see his nieces and nephews grow up… All Pac got was a death sentence."

Davis was arrested in 2023, years after repeatedly placing himself in the car on the night of the shooting — first in interviews, later in his 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend. He has consistently said he was not the shooter. By his own account, the attack was payback for an assault on his nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, at an MGM Grand boxing match in Las Vegas hours earlier, which itself followed a Los Angeles fight involving Anderson and an associate of Death Row Records founder Suge Knight.

As Pitchfork noted in its report on the sentencing, Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in closing arguments that Davis "went hunting" for Shakur and Knight that night. The two were shot while stopped at a red light. Knight survived his injuries; Shakur, who was 25, died six days later. Davis is the last living person among the four men prosecutors identified as occupants of the Cadillac.

A 2008 interview conducted under a proffer agreement became central evidence against him. Davis told investigators that Anderson fired the fatal shots — "He rolled down the window, popped 'em," he said, adding, "If they drove on my side, I would have popped 'em." Davis had assumed the agreement shielded him from discussing the murder publicly. It was later voided, and prosecutors used his own words in building the case.

items.title: Michael Jackson’s Famed Super Bowl Halftime Show Performance Captured in New Documentary
items.summary:
Michael Jackson's 1993 Super Bowl halftime show is getting the documentary treatment. Spectacle: Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl, a new series, will arrive on Hulu and ESPN in February 2027.

Jackson performed at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena during Super Bowl XXVII on January 31, 1993, a set widely credited with transforming the halftime slot from a scheduling obligation into a stage worth chasing. It remains a fixture on lists of the best halftime performances ever staged. The documentary digs into how the show came together, drawing on footage that has not been seen publicly and on reflections about what the performance set in motion.

The first official trailer is out now, Consequence reported. The series is timed to land ahead of Super Bowl LXI, which the NFL will hold at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles on February 14, 2027.

That game marks a shift in how the Super Bowl reaches viewers. ABC will carry the broadcast, and for the first time the game will also air on ESPN and stream on Disney+ — the same corporate family that will house the Jackson documentary a few weeks earlier.

items.title: ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ Trailer: Greta Gerwig’s Fantasy Epic Unveils Aslan, the White Witch and More in Dazzling Footage
items.summary:
Netflix released the first trailer for Narnia: The Magician's Nephew on Tuesday, giving audiences an early look at Greta Gerwig's adaptation of C.S. Lewis' novel. The film follows Digory and Polly, two children who become the first to find the Wood between the Worlds, and it arrives in theaters on February 12, 2027 before streaming on Netflix starting April 2.

The trailer, scored to Led Zeppelin's "Stairway to Heaven," opens with Daniel Craig as Andrew Ketterley, the magician of the title, handing the children a ring that carries them across worlds. It introduces Emma Mackey as Jadis, the future White Witch and last Queen of Charn, and Meryl Streep's Aslan, singing Narnia into being. Carey Mulligan and Ciarán Hinds also appear, with newcomers David McKenna and Beatrice Campbell in the lead roles.

According to Variety, Netflix previewed the trailer for press at New York's AMC Lincoln Square, where Stephen Colbert interviewed Gerwig about the adaptation. She traced the project back to a cocktail party around the 2019 release of her husband Noah Baumbach's Marriage Story, a year after Netflix acquired the Narnia rights. "I made a beeline for Ted Sarandos at a cocktail party and said, 'I really think you should start with The Magician's Nephew,'" Gerwig said. "About 20 minutes later he said, 'Do you want to write it?' At that point, I had only made Lady Bird and Little Women. I hadn't done Barbie yet."

Lewis published The Magician's Nephew in 1955, five years after The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, and later said he wanted readers to begin with the prequel. The books were adapted as a BBC miniseries from 1988 to 1990 and as three films from Disney and 20th Century between 2005 and 2010.

Getting Led Zeppelin's blessing took persuasion. Gerwig wrote to Robert Plant and Jimmy Page and showed them an early cut before the band agreed to license the song. "It's an epic song, and narratively, about a spiritual journey, a path of fake idols and wrong roads you can go down," she said. "I was so moved that they allowed me to use this song."

The film is Gerwig's first since Barbie in 2023 and Netflix's first movie to get a global theatrical release — a condition she pushed for. "I told Ted I only know how to make movies for the big screen," she said. "He said, 'Make the movie for the biggest screen and trust the process.'"
